name: Grounds For Thought: August Lineup
description: Grounds for Thought: August 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesFour Thursday evenings. Four very different conversations. Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shops. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does.6th August: Shambhavi TiwariPossessed: The Ghost, The Asylum, The Priest, and the PeopleWhen someone in rural India is "possessed by a ghost," they encounter not just their family and their priest, but eventually — often — a psychiatrist. Two completely different frameworks for what has gone wrong, and what healing looks like. This session uses spirit possession across Indian cultural contexts to examine what happens when indigenous knowledge systems and clinical medicine cross paths. PhD researcher Shambhavi Tiwari, who has spent years in this space, asks: superstition, myth, knowledge system, or something else entirely?13th August: Dr. Vishwas ChitaleZoom In, Zoom Out: What India's Climate Risk Looks Like at Ground LevelEveryone has heard the national climate numbers. But zoom into a district, and the picture changes entirely — neighbouring areas with opposite risk profiles, and disaster plans built on averages too coarse to catch where the real danger sits. Dr. Vishwas Chitale, Fellow at CEEW, will walk us through India's climate risk from the national level down to your own neighbourhood — and then hand the tool to the room. Participants will pull up their own hometown's actual climate risk profile live, using CRAVIS, CEEW's climate intelligence platform. You'll leave having done a small piece of the research yourself.20th August: Antara ChakrabartyFrom Village to Viral: How Folk Music Got a Second LifeA seventeenth-century Sufi verse now has a hundred million YouTube views. The songs of Lalon Fakir, Bengal's wandering poet-saint, are uniting two Bengals and two centuries through a single melody. This session traces folk music's remarkable journey — from Punjab's Sufi shrines and Bengal's riverside Baul gatherings to studio stages and streaming platforms — and asks the questions nobody quite wants to answer. Who owns a folk song? What happens when heritage becomes entertainment? Does something get lost in translation, or does it simply learn a new way to survive? Expect live music, a few surprises, and a fresh way of listening to songs you may already love.27th August: Sunaina SaxenaWhat is a Clean Street Worth?Why are two seemingly identical houses priced so differently? This session explores one of environmental economics' most elegant tools, hedonic pricing, to answer a question most of us have never thought to ask: does the cleanliness of a neighbourhood have a measurable economic value? Through stories, discussion, and simple examples, researcher Sunaina Saxena explores how clean streets, reliable waste collection, and a healthy living environment become embedded in housing prices — and what that reveals about our cities and the choices we make about where we live.

name: Forwarded as Received: Misinformation 101
description: Join us for a lecture that asks a question with no comfortable answer:If the people deciding what counts as true are working from the same broken information as everyone else, who do we trust to hold the line?About The Lecture"Fake news" was always too small a phrase. It suggested a fabricated story, a fact-check, a correction — a problem that could, in theory, be solved. What we're actually living through is something else: real photographs stripped of context, selective truths, political insinuation, and claims repeated in enough WhatsApp groups until they stop needing to be true at all.Drawing on her book "Forwarded as Received: How Misinformation Turns Viral, Violent and True," this lecture looks past the individual act of falling for a hoax and toward the larger machinery — how misinformation and malinformation move through digital platforms, political campaigns, and even bureaucratic institutions, shaping not just what people believe, but who gets counted, trusted, or excluded.This isn't a lecture about how other people get fooled. It's about how the very systems built to establish "the facts" — platforms, institutions, public systems — can become vulnerable to the same distortions they claim to correct.About the SpeakerSaadia Azim is the author of "Forwarded as Received: How Misinformation Turns Viral, Violent and True" (Simon & Schuster India), which examines how misinformation moves through everyday social behaviour, politics, media and technology to acquire the force of public truth. She is Chief Operating Officer of the Government of West Bengal's Digital Public Service Delivery Programme, a former journalist, and an Internet Society Mid-Career Fellow. Her work focuses on misinformation, digital governance, algorithmic power, public trust and democratic behaviour in India and the Global South.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

description: Join us for a lecture that traces one dangerous idea through three brilliant, broken minds:In 1891, Georg Cantor gave us set theory, and then spent years battling for his peace of mind. description: Nani ka Ghar by V's Supper Stories A supper brunch of home-cooked nostalgia.Some recipes don't survive migration. They get left behind in old kitchens, remembered only in fragments-  a smell, a story, a dish someone's grandmother used to make that no one quite knows how to recreate anymore.Nani ka Ghar is a supper built around dishes like that. Rooted in Multan, where my own Nani is from, and reaching into Lahore and Sindh - the homes our grandparents carried with them.  This menu brings back food that's slow, laborious, and increasingly rare: a sourdough flatbread fermented over three days, a lotus-stem starter barely made anymore even in Sindhi households, a moth dal kachori you'll mostly only find on a handful of old Delhi streets.Alongside them sit the dishes that never left,  a rich Lahori chicken karahi, a comforting channay, and phirni made exactly the way it's made every Holi in our family, because some things don't need reviving. They just need to be shared.Come hungry. Come with stories of your own kitchens, if you have them.Date - 13th September Time - 12:30pm - 3pm A limited seating supper.
